metadata.title: Verifying Private AI Valuations
metadata.purpose: Week 1 progress update (Mycroft project) for a new agent, the Private AI Valuation Agent: can private AI company share prices actually be recovered from SEC Form N-PORT filings, what broke when the plan met real data, and what the frozen universe looks like. Audience: professor / project review. Voice: free local Kokoro. This is the first video in a new project series, not a continuation of the Hacker News AI Buzz Tracker arc.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video covers week one of my Private AI Valuation Agent, a new Mycroft project. It covers what I verified by hand from real SEC filings, two defects I found in my own plan before writing any pipeline code, and the universe I froze as a result.

Most of the AI industry's value sits in companies you cannot buy. OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks. No ticker, no earnings call, no public price. But the mutual funds that own pieces of them have to report every holding to the SEC, with a dollar value and a share count. Divide one by the other and you get a price per share for a company that has no public price.

props.headline: A price for companies that have no price

beats.narration_text: In week one I verified that by hand. I pulled nineteen Anthropic positions from six different fund families straight out of the filings and did the arithmetic myself. Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Alger and ARK all priced Anthropic at two hundred fifty nine dollars and fourteen cents. Identical, to the cent. Then a new funding round repriced it, and BlackRock and Capital Group both marked it at five eighty nine, matching to four decimal places, two days apart.

Then I hit the problems. My plan had a filter that was supposed to isolate private holdings. It dropped five of my six managers, silently, with no error. Different funds write N slash A or nine zeros for a missing identifier, and two of them flag restricted stock as unrestricted. The plan also expected a few thousand private rows per quarter. The real number was six hundred and six thousand. So I inverted the pipeline. Match companies by name first, confirm they are private second. That shrank the hardest part of the project by about six hundred times.

So the output for week one. The approach is proven. The SEC's bulk data matched my hand read filings fifteen out of fifteen, exactly. And universe version one is frozen at six companies, with SpaceX added, and Cohere removed, because every single Cohere match turned out to be Coherent Corp, a public optics company.
Next week: load eight quarters into the database, and start on entity resolution.
